steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on LoRe, a programming model for local-first software with verified safety properties. Motivate local-first applications, explain why CRDT-based approaches aren't enough, describe the model's building blocks, relate it to coordination avoidance work, and list our contributions.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Collaborative applications over unreliable networks
  - apps where multiple parties on partially unreliable networks process data collaboratively are everywhere
  - example: distributed calendar app: add/modify appointments, multiple calendars on different devices, sharing, cloud backup
  - must be accessible offline (e.g. traveling); planning may need coordination between parties
  - representative of group collaboration tools, digital (cross-organizational) supply chains, multiplayer online gaming
- Centralized architecture and its problems
  - dominating architecture: centralized, data in data centers, edge devices = interfaces
  - simplifies edge software: consistency/safety managed centrally
  - issues: loss of control over data ownership and privacy, poor offline availability, latency, inefficient use of communication infrastructure, wasted (powerful) edge computing
- Local-first software and the gap in existing approaches
  - local-first principles: move data management/processing to edge devices instead of clouds
  - to be viable: need automatically verifiable safety guarantees to replace centralized assumptions
  - Yjs, Automerge: no such guarantees
  - use CRDTs for shared state + callbacks for state changing in time and space
  - CRDTs from geo-replicated databases; off-the-shelf databases or libraries
  - strongest CRDT consistency = causal consistency; not enough for invariants needing coordination (vacation days example)
  - delimit coordination: [quote: Brewer on maximizing combinations of availability and consistency]
  - need to reason about interleavings of data flows end-to-end: interface -> device-local dependency chains -> remote devices and back
  - unpredictable concurrent interactions + no central authority + implicit callback dependencies -> error-prone without automation
- Our programming model: reactives, invariants, interactions
  - programming model for local-first apps with explicit safety properties, enforced automatically
  - reactives: values changing in time and in space (replicated); systematic treatment of state, dependencies, concurrent changes; functional composition
  - invariants: first-order logic formulas, must hold whenever app interacts with outside world or reactive values observable
  - interactions: interface to outside world, encapsulate changes to all affected reactives (direct state, derived local values, shared remote state)
  - language-managed cross-device data flows, best-in-class consistency
  - on one device: logically instantaneous, no intermediate states (like atomicity in databases)
  - automatic verification with invariants as obligations -> find interactions needing coordination; compiler generates protocol; others visible in causal order
  - -> application-specific availability-safety trade-off
- Relation to coordination avoidance
  - availability-safety trade-off explored in systems/database community as "coordination avoidance"
  - user-specified invariants to synthesize distributed objects or configure per-operation consistency
  - difference (1): peer-to-peer local-first, no central authority, offline availability, interactions with outside world
  - difference (2): not programming against datastore/object interface (two tiers: monolithic store + application tier) but language-integrated mixed consistency, whole-program guarantees, safety of derived data “all the way down”
  - needed because complexity in local-first comes from interactions with external world, handled in application logic
- Contributions
  - (1) LoRe programming model with verified safety (Section 2); CRDTs, reactives not novel but repurposed/combined/extended
  - (2) formal definition: invariant preservation, confluence for interactions, modular verification; invariants about sequential behaviour; automatic coordination on potential violation (Section 3)
  - (3) verifying compiler: LoRe -> Viper (verification) and Scala (application logic + synthesized synchronization) (Section 4)
  - (4) evaluation, two case studies (Section 5): (a) facilitates safe local-first software, (b) efficient modular verification; costs not prohibitive

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Today there are many applications that let multiple parties, connected over partially unreliable networks, process data collaboratively. One example is a distributed calendar application with services for adding or modifying appointments. A user may keep multiple calendars on different devices, may share calendars with other users, and back them up in a cloud. Calendars must be accessible to users in many scenarios, including offline periods, e.g., while traveling, but planning appointments may need coordination between multiple parties. The calendar application is representative of other collaborative data-driven software, like group collaboration tools, digital (cross-organizational) supply chains, multiplayer online gaming, and more.

The dominating software architecture for these applications is centralized. Data is collected, managed, and processed centrally in data centers, and devices on the edge of the communication infrastructure mainly serve as interfaces to users and the outside world. This architecture makes the software on edge devices simpler, because concerns like consistent data changes for ensuring safety properties are handled centrally. But it also has issues, including loss of control over data ownership and privacy, insufficient offline availability, poor latency, inefficient use of communication infrastructure, and wasting (powerful) computing resources on the edge.

To address these issues, local-first principles for software development were formulated, which call for moving data management and processing to edge devices instead of keeping the data in clouds. But programming approaches that implement these principles can only be viable alternatives to the centralized approach if they support automatically verifiable safety guarantees, to make up for the simplifying assumptions that a centralized approach allows. Unfortunately, existing approaches for programming local-first applications such as Yjs or Automerge do not give such guarantees. They use conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) to store the parts of their state that are shared across devices, and they rely on callbacks for modeling and managing state that changes in both time and space. CRDTs were invented in the context of geo-replicated databases and are available as off-the-shelf databases or libraries. But causal consistency, which is the strongest consistency level that CRDTs ensure, is not enough to maintain invariants that need coordination among the participants, for example the invariant that employees should not enter more than the available vacation days when the calendar app is used in a business setting. At the same time we need to limit the scope of coordination so as to “maximize combinations of availability and consistency that make sense for a particular application”. In a local-first setting, to find the set of interactions that really need coordination, one has to reason about possible interleavings of their data flows "end-to-end", i.e., from the interface to the outside world, through device-local data-dependency chains, to remote devices and back. The interactions triggered by the outside world are unpredictable and happen concurrently at different devices, there is no central authority, and current callback-centered programming models have implicit dependencies everywhere. All this makes such reasoning without automated support challenging and error-prone.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Today there are many applications that let multiple parties, connected over partially unreliable networks, process data collaboratively. One example is a distributed calendar application with services for adding or modifying appointments. A user may keep multiple calendars on different devices, may share calendars with other users, and back them up in a cloud. Calendars must be accessible to users in many scenarios, including offline periods, e.g., while traveling, but planning appointments may need coordination between multiple parties. The calendar application is representative of other collaborative data-driven software, like group collaboration tools, digital (cross-organizational) supply chains, multiplayer online gaming, and more.

The dominating software architecture for these applications is centralized. Data is collected, managed, and processed centrally in data centers, and devices on the edge of the communication infrastructure mainly serve as interfaces to users and the outside world. This architecture makes the software on edge devices simpler, because concerns like consistent data changes for ensuring safety properties are handled centrally. But it also has issues, including loss of control over data ownership and privacy, insufficient offline availability, poor latency, inefficient use of communication infrastructure, and wasting (powerful) computing resources on the edge.

To address these issues, local-first principles for software development were formulated, which call for moving data management and processing to edge devices instead of keeping the data in clouds. But programming approaches that implement these principles can only be viable alternatives to the centralized approach if they support automatically verifiable safety guarantees, to make up for the simplifying assumptions that a centralized approach allows. Unfortunately, existing approaches for programming local-first applications such as Yjs or Automerge do not give such guarantees. They use conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) to store the parts of their state that are shared across devices, and they rely on callbacks for modeling and managing state that changes in both time and space. CRDTs were invented in the context of geo-replicated databases and are available as off-the-shelf databases or libraries. But causal consistency, which is the strongest consistency level that CRDTs ensure, is not enough to maintain invariants that need coordination among the participants, for example the invariant that employees should not enter more than the available vacation days when the calendar app is used in a business setting. At the same time we need to limit the scope of coordination so as to “maximize combinations of availability and consistency that make sense for a particular application”. In a local-first setting, to find the set of interactions that really need coordination, one has to reason about possible interleavings of their data flows "end-to-end", i.e., from the interface to the outside world, through device-local data-dependency chains, to remote devices and back. The interactions triggered by the outside world are unpredictable and happen concurrently at different devices, there is no central authority, and current callback-centered programming models have implicit dependencies everywhere. All this makes such reasoning without automated support challenging and error-prone.

To close this gap, we propose a programming model for local-first applications that has explicit safety properties and enforces them automatically. The model has three core building blocks: reactives, invariants, and interactions. Reactives express values that change in time, but also in space, because they are replicated over multiple devices. They allow complex state, dependencies, and concurrent changes to be treated systematically, so developers can reason in terms of functional composition. Invariants are formulas in first-order logic that specify safety properties, which must hold at all times when the application interacts with the outside world or when values of reactives are observable. Interactions are the interface to the outside world and they encapsulate the changes to all reactives that are affected by interacting with it (state that the interactions change directly, device-local values derived from the changed state, and shared state at remote devices). They act as language-managed cross-device data flows that automatically use best-in-class consistency. On one device, interactions are logically processed instantaneously, i.e., no intermediate states can be observed, similar to atomicity in databases. We use automatic verification, with the invariants as verification obligations, to find the interactions that need coordination across devices, and the compiler generates the coordination protocol for them; all other interactions become visible in causal order. In this way the compiler makes an availability-safety trade-off that is specific to the application.

The systems and database community has explored the availability-safety trade-off under the term "coordination avoidance", and there are approaches that use safety invariants specified by the user to synthesize distributed objects or to configure the right consistency level for each database operation. Our work takes inspiration from these approaches, but it differs in two key aspects. (1) We target a peer-to-peer local-first setting, not geo-replicated databases, and this has unique challenges; specifically, we do not assume any centralized authority, and we have offline availability and interactions with the outside world. (2) Applications are not programmed against the interface of a distributed datastore/object, which leads to designs split into two separate tiers – an automatically managed monolithic data store and the application tier that uses the API of the store. Instead we provide language-integrated mixed consistency with whole program guarantees, i.e., we verify the safety of derived data “all the way down”. This is needed in a local-first setting, because there most of the complexity comes from interactions with the external world, and these are handled as part of the application logic, not as part of the data store.

To summarize, our contributions are:

- (1) A programming model for local-first applications with verified safety properties, called LoRe (Section 2). Individual elements of the model, like CRDTs or reactives, are not new, but they are repurposed, combined, and extended in a unique way to systematically address the specific needs of local-first applications when it comes to ensuring safety properties.

- (2) A formal definition of the model, including a formal notion of invariant preservation and confluence for interactions, and a modular verification that invariants are never violated. In particular, our model allows invariants that reason about the sequential behaviour of the program. If an invariant could be violated because of concurrent execution, LoRe adds the necessary coordination logic automatically (Section 3).

- (3) A verifying compiler that translates LoRe programs to Viper for automated verification, and to Scala for the application logic, including synthesized synchronization that guarantees the specified safety invariants (Section 4).

- (4) An evaluation of LoRe in two case studies (Section 5). The evaluation validates two claims we make about the proposed programming model: (a) it makes it easier to develop safe local-first software, and (b) it allows efficient and modular verification of safety properties. It also shows that the additional safety properties of our model do not come with prohibitive costs in verification effort and time.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Applications that enable multiple parties connected via partially unreliable networks to collaboratively process data are prevalent today. An illustrative example is a distributed calendar application with services to add or modify appointments, where a user may maintain multiple calendars on different devices, share calendars with other users, and back them up in a cloud; calendars must be accessible to users in a variety of scenarios, including offline periods, e.g., while traveling – yet planning appointments may require coordination between multiple parties. The calendar application is representative of other collaborative data-driven software such as group collaboration tools, digital (cross-organizational) supply chains, multiplayer online gaming, and more.

The dominating software architecture for such applications is centralized: data is collected, managed, and processed centrally in data centers, while devices on the edge of the communication infrastructure serve primarily as interfaces to users and the outside world. This architecture simplifies the software running on edge devices, since concerns like consistent data changes to ensure safety properties are managed centrally. However, it comes with issues including loss of control over data ownership and privacy, insufficient offline availability, poor latency, inefficient use of communication infrastructure, and waste of (powerful) computing resources on the edge.

To address these issues, local-first principles for software development have been formulated [1], calling for moving data management and processing to edge devices instead of confining data to clouds. But for programming approaches that implement these principles to be viable alternatives to the centralized approach, they must support automatically verifiable safety guarantees to make up for the simplifying assumptions afforded by centralization. Unfortunately, existing approaches to programming local-first applications such as Yjs [2] or Automerge [3] do not provide such guarantees. They use conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) [4] to store the parts of their state that are shared across devices and rely on callbacks for modeling and managing state that changes in both time and space. CRDTs were invented in the context of geo-replicated databases and are available as off-the-shelf databases [5] or libraries [6,7]. But the strongest consistency level ensured by CRDTs, causal consistency [8], is not enough to maintain invariants that require coordination among participants, e.g., the invariant that employees should not enter more than the available vacation days when the calendar app is used in a business setting. At the same time, we need to delimit the scope of coordination so as to “maximize combinations of availability and consistency that make sense for a particular application” [9]. To find the set of interactions that actually need coordination in a local-first setting, one must reason about possible interleavings of their data flows "end-to-end", i.e., from the interface to the outside world, through device-local data-dependency chains, to remote devices and back. The unpredictability of interactions triggered by the outside world concurrently at different devices, together with the absence of a central authority and the prevailing implicit dependencies in current callback-centered programming models, makes such reasoning without automated support a challenging, error-prone endeavour.

To close this gap, we propose a programming model for local-first applications that features explicit safety properties and enforces them automatically. The model has three core building blocks: reactives, invariants, and interactions. Reactives express values that change in time, but also in space, by being replicated over multiple devices. They enable systematic treatment of complex state, dependencies, and concurrent changes, letting developers reason in terms of functional composition. Invariants are formulas in first-order logic specifying safety properties that must hold at all times when the application interacts with the outside world or when values of reactives are observable. Interactions interface to the outside world and encapsulate changes to all reactives affected by interactions with it (state directly changed by the interactions, device-local values derived from the changed state, and shared state at remote devices). They serve as language-managed cross-device data flows that automatically use best-in-class consistency. On a single device, interactions are logically processed instantaneously, i.e., no intermediate states are observable, similar to atomicity in databases. We use automatic verification with invariants as verification obligations to identify the interactions that need coordination across devices, for which the compiler generates the coordination protocol; all other interactions become visible in causal order. This way, the compiler makes an application-specific availability-safety trade-off.

The availability-safety trade-off has been explored in the systems and database community under the term "coordination avoidance", and there are approaches that leverage user-specified safety invariants to synthesize distributed objects or to correctly configure the consistency level of each database operation [10,11,12,13]. Our work draws inspiration from these approaches but differs in two key aspects: (1) Instead of geo-replicated databases, we target a peer-to-peer local-first setting with unique challenges; specifically, we assume no centralized authority and feature offline availability and interactions with the outside world. (2) Instead of programming applications against the interface of a distributed datastore/object, which fosters designs split into two separate tiers – an automatically managed monolithic data store and the application tier using the store’s API – we provide language-integrated mixed consistency with whole program guarantees, i.e., we verify the safety of derived data “all the way down”. This is necessary in a local-first setting, where most of the complexity arises from interactions with the external world, which are handled as part of the application logic rather than the data store.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

- (1) A programming model for local-first applications with verified safety properties, called LoRe (Section 2). While individual elements of the model, e.g., CRDTs or reactives, are not novel, they are repurposed, combined, and extended in a unique way to systematically address the specific needs of local-first applications regarding safety properties.

- (2) A formal definition of the model, including a formal notion of invariant preservation and confluence for interactions, and a modular verification that invariants are never violated. In particular, our model enables invariants that reason about the sequential behaviour of the program. In case of potential invariant violations due to concurrent execution, LoRe automatically adds the necessary coordination logic (Section 3).

- (3) A verifying compiler that translates LoRe programs to Viper [14] for automated verification and to Scala for the application logic, including synthesized synchronization to guarantee the specified safety invariants (Section 4).

- (4) An evaluation of LoRe in two case studies (Section 5). Our evaluation validates two claims about the proposed programming model: (a) it facilitates the development of safe local-first software, and (b) it enables efficient and modular verification of safety properties. It further shows that the additional safety properties offered by our model do not come with prohibitive costs in verification effort and time.
